description: Becker on labelling, deviant careers and moral entrepreneurs. How labels create and sustain deviance.
content_html:
The Interactionist Challenge

Functionalist and structural theories ask why certain social conditions (strain, status frustration, class inequality) lead to crime. Interactionist sociology asks a different question: who decides what counts as criminal or deviant in the first place, and what happens to individuals once they are labelled? This shift of focus — from the causes of rule-breaking to the social processes of labelling — produced one of the most influential perspectives in the sociology of crime.

Interactionism argues that social reality is constructed through interaction and the meanings people assign to actions. Applied to crime and deviance, this means that an act has no inherent criminal quality — it becomes deviant only when someone with the power to make the label stick successfully defines it as such.

Becker: Labelling Theory

Howard Becker, in Outsiders (1963), set out the foundational argument of labelling theory. Becker argued that deviance is not a property of the act itself but of the interaction between the person who acts and those who observe and respond to the act. Whether a label of “deviant” or “criminal” is applied depends on who commits the act, when and where it is committed, who observes it, and the negotiations between the various parties involved.

Becker observed that not all rule-breakers are caught, and not all who are caught are labelled. Whether a label sticks depends on factors beyond the act itself: the social characteristics of the actor (class, ethnicity, age, gender), the discretion of those with formal power (police, teachers, courts), and the social context. Two young people committing the same act may receive very different responses depending on where they are and who they are. Becker’s insight was that the criminal justice system is not a neutral machine but a social process shaped by power.

Key Fact

Becker (Outsiders, 1963) argued that deviance is not a property of the act but is created by the reactions of others. An act only becomes deviant when a label is successfully applied by someone with the power to make it stick.

Master Status and the Deviant Career

Once a label has been publicly and officially applied, Becker argued, it tends to become the person’s master status. Before the label, a young person might be seen as a student, a friend, a neighbour. After being officially convicted and labelled a “criminal”, this identity overshadows all others. Assumptions are made about the person’s character, reliability and likely future behaviour — assumptions that can follow them into every interaction: with employers, with landlords, with teachers, with family members.

The consequences of master status may trigger what Becker described as a deviant career. As the labelled individual is rejected from legitimate social roles — turned down by employers, excluded from educational opportunities, cut off from conventional social networks — the label itself makes conventional life harder to sustain. This rejection can produce a self-fulfilling prophecy: the individual increasingly identifies with the label and seeks out others who share it, joining organised deviant groups with their own norms, values and identity. In this way, the labelling process can transform an isolated act of rule-breaking into an ongoing criminal lifestyle — not because the individual was inevitably going to become a criminal, but because the social reaction created the conditions for it.

Primary and Secondary Deviance

Primary deviance refers to the original act of rule-breaking, before any label has been applied. Most people commit acts of primary deviance at some point (minor theft, underage drinking, breaking traffic rules) without it becoming part of their identity. Secondary deviance occurs when an individual internalises the deviant label and begins to act in accordance with it. The distinction is important: the theory argues that secondary deviance is produced not by the original act but by the social reaction to it.

Moral Entrepreneurs and Moral Panics

Becker also introduced the concept of moral entrepreneurs — individuals and groups who use their social influence to get particular behaviours defined as deviant. They may lobby parliament for new legislation, campaign in the media, or pressure institutions to act. Their success depends on their social power and their ability to frame the issue in ways that resonate with public anxieties.

Related to this is the concept of a moral panic. When the media, police and public respond to a perceived threat in a disproportionate and amplified way, the resulting attention can itself increase the visible scale of the problem through a process of deviancy amplification: increased police attention leads to more arrests, which generates more media coverage, which fuels further anxiety and policing. The labelling process escalates. Critics argue that moral panics have historically targeted specific groups (young working-class men, ethnic minority communities) who are portrayed as “folk devils” — symbols of social threat.

Feminist perspective: Feminist sociologists broadly welcome the insight that labelling is not neutral. Heidensohn noted that the criminal justice system has historically applied labels differently to men and women: women offenders are sometimes treated more leniently (the “chivalry thesis”) when they conform to feminine stereotypes, but women who deviate from expected gender roles may be judged more harshly. Feminist criminologists argue that the identity of the label-appliers — predominantly male judges, police and juries — shapes who is targeted and how they are treated.

Marxist perspective: Marxist sociologists argue that labelling theory does not go far enough because it focuses on individual interactions without asking why the police and courts are more likely to label working-class people as criminal. The answer, for Marxists, lies in the class structure: the bourgeoisie controls the legal system and ensures that the label “criminal” is attached primarily to acts associated with the proletariat (street crime, theft, benefit fraud) rather than to the far more costly but largely tolerated crimes of the powerful (corporate fraud, tax avoidance, environmental damage). Selective law enforcement reflects and reinforces class inequality.

Key Fact

Labelling theory has been criticised from multiple directions: Marxists argue it doesn’t explain why labels fall on the working class (class power); feminists argue gender shapes both labelling and its consequences; critics also note that not everyone who is labelled accepts or acts on the label (determinism).

Strengths: Labelling theory challenges the view that crime statistics are an objective reflection of criminal behaviour, showing instead that they reflect the activities of the police and courts. It draws attention to the unequal application of labels across social groups. It helps explain patterns such as recidivism (re-offending after conviction), which purely structural theories struggle to account for.

Weaknesses: Labelling theory has been criticised for being too deterministic — not everyone who is labelled becomes a career criminal; many labelled individuals resist and reject the identity. It focuses on the label-givers (police, courts) but underplays the role of the actor’s own choices and motivations. Functionalists argue that labelling theory cannot explain why some acts (serious violence) are universally condemned regardless of the social identity of the actor.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe question about labelling theory, students often describe what a label is but neglect to explain what it does — the consequences of master status, the self-fulfilling prophecy, and the deviant career. A strong 4-mark answer needs both: the process of labelling (who applies labels, under what conditions) and its consequences (master status reshapes how others respond; self-fulfilling prophecy reshapes the individual’s own identity). For the 12-mark Discuss, the highest-scoring answers will compare labelling theory with at least one other perspective — e.g. contrasting Becker’s focus on the reaction of others with Merton’s focus on structural strain, or with the Marxist point that labelling reflects class power. Always end with a supported judgement that weighs the evidence.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Becker’s labelling theory (Outsiders, 1963) argues that deviance is not a quality of the act but is created by the social reaction to it. An act becomes deviant when a powerful audience successfully labels it as such.
  • Once labelled, a person may acquire a master status that overrides all other identities, triggering a deviant career through the self-fulfilling prophecy as they are excluded from conventional roles and drawn into organised deviant groups.
  • Marxists and feminists extend labelling theory: Marxists argue class power determines who gets labelled; feminists argue gender shapes both who is targeted and how they are treated. Both perspectives challenge the interactionist focus on individual interaction without addressing structural inequality.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the concept of 'master status' in labelling theory?
A) The highest rank a person can achieve in the social hierarchy
B) A label that overrides all other social identities and becomes the primary way others see the person
C) The first deviant act committed by an individual
D) The process by which crime statistics are collected by the police
practice_questions.marks: B) A label that overrides all other social identities and becomes the primary way others see the person [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what sociologists mean by the term 'labelling'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that labelling is the process by which an act or person is defined as deviant or criminal by others. 1 mark for extending this: e.g. Becker argued that whether the label is applied depends not just on the act itself but on who commits it, who observes it, and the power of those doing the labelling; the label then shapes how others interact with the person.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe how a deviant career may develop following the application of a criminal label.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the deviant career as the process by which a labelled individual is drawn progressively further into a deviant identity. 2 marks for a developed description including: the labelled person is excluded from legitimate opportunities (employment, housing, education) because the master status precedes them; this makes conventional life harder, producing a self-fulfilling prophecy; the individual increasingly identifies with the label and joins organised deviant groups with their own values and norms, completing what Becker called the deviant career.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a Marxist sociologist might criticise labelling theory's explanation of crime.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying the Marxist perspective and its focus on class and power. 1 mark for identifying that Marxists agree labels are not applied equally but argue that labelling theory doesn't explain why. 1 mark for explaining the Marxist answer: the bourgeoisie controls the legal system and directs enforcement against working-class acts (street crime, benefit fraud) while failing to prosecute or under-penalising the crimes of the powerful (corporate fraud, tax avoidance). 1 mark for connecting this to selective law enforcement: the label 'criminal' is attached disproportionately to the proletariat, reinforcing class inequality and protecting ruling-class interests.

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that it is the reaction of others, not the act itself, that makes someone a criminal. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Strong evaluation of labelling theory with reference to Becker (Outsiders, 1963), master status, self-fulfilling prophecy, deviant career, moral entrepreneurs. Arguments in support: interactionist evidence that the same act receives different labels depending on who commits it and who observes; crime statistics reflect policing practices as much as actual offending (dark figure of crime); deviancy amplification through moral panics shows how reactions escalate labelling. Arguments against: Merton's strain theory argues that structural conditions (not reactions) cause crime; Marxist critique (labelling doesn't explain class-based patterns of policing without reference to class power); feminist critique (gender shapes labelling in ways interactionists underexplain); functionalists argue some acts are universally condemned regardless of who commits them. Student names at least Becker plus one contrasting perspective and reaches a supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered with named theorists, judgement present.

Developing: Mostly one perspective with limited evaluation, some theorists named.

Emerging: Basic descriptions, few theorists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the difference between primary and secondary deviance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying primary deviance as initial rule-breaking before a label is publicly applied. 1 mark for correctly identifying secondary deviance as the deviance that results from internalising the label and acting in accordance with the deviant identity. 1 mark for making the distinction clear: primary deviance does not alter the individual's self-identity; secondary deviance arises from the social reaction to the act and produces a fundamental shift in how the labelled person sees themselves and behaves.

knowledge_checks.q: According to Becker, what is the primary factor that determines whether an act becomes labelled as deviant?
options: The seriousness of harm caused by the act
The social class of the person who commits the act
Whether the act breaks a formal law
The reaction and labelling process of others with the power to make the label stick

knowledge_checks.q: Which concept describes the period of public anxiety in which a group is portrayed as a threat to social values, often out of proportion to the actual threat?
In labelling theory, _____ deviance is the original rule-breaking act before any label has been publicly applied.
Becker called the label that overrides all other social identities the _____ status.
Match each concept to its definition:
right: The process by which a labelled person is progressively excluded from conventional roles and drawn into a deviant lifestyle
A person who campaigns to have certain behaviours defined as deviant or criminal
When a person comes to behave in the way predicted by a label applied to them

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote 'Outsiders' and in what year?
What is labelling theory's core claim about deviance?
flashcard_questions.a: Deviance is not a property of the act itself but is created by the reactions and labels applied by others.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a master status, according to Becker?
flashcard_questions.a: A label that overrides all other social identities and becomes the primary way others see and respond to a person.
The process by which a labelled person is excluded from conventional roles, internalises the label and is drawn deeper into deviance.
An initial rule-breaking act before any label has been publicly applied, so it does not change the person's identity.
Deviance that results from internalising a label and acting in accordance with the deviant identity it imposes.
People or groups who campaign to have certain behaviours defined as deviant or criminal, using media and lobbying.
A period of disproportionate public anxiety in which a group is defined as a threat to social values, often amplified by the media.
The process by which increased policing and media attention escalates the visible scale of a deviant group's behaviour.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Marxist criticism of labelling theory?
flashcard_questions.a: It describes unequal labelling but does not explain why — class power directs labelling at the working class.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the self-fulfilling prophecy in labelling theory?
flashcard_questions.a: When a person begins to behave in line with a label, confirming the expectations the label created in others.

flashcard_questions.q: What is interactionism's key focus in studying crime?
flashcard_questions.a: Small-scale labelling processes and the meanings attached to acts, rather than large-scale structural causes.

glossary_terms.definition: A sociological perspective that focuses on small-scale face-to-face interactions and the meanings people attach to their own and others' behaviour.
The process by which an act or person is publicly defined as deviant or criminal by others, particularly those with institutional power.
A label that overrides all other social identities, becoming the primary way in which others see and respond to a person.
The process by which a labelled person is progressively excluded from conventional roles and drawn further into a deviant identity and lifestyle.
When a person begins to act in the way predicted by a label applied to them, confirming the expectations the label created in others.
A person or group that campaigns to have certain behaviours defined as deviant or criminal, often through media pressure and lobbying for legislation.
A period of disproportionate public anxiety in which a group is portrayed as a threat to social values, typically amplified by media coverage.
An initial rule-breaking act before any public label has been applied, so it does not alter the individual's social identity.
Deviance that results from internalising a publicly applied label and beginning to act in accordance with the deviant identity it imposes.

hero_image_caption: Labelling theory shifts the focus from 'why do people break rules?' to 'who has the power to decide what counts as rule-breaking?'
